a2-unit-04.04.1 Radio show:
Host: Good morning Chicago, and welcome to Chicago Talks. We all love our phones, but are they making us unhappy? My guest today is psychologist Dr. Alan Brooks. Welcome to the show!
Doctor: Thank you. It's great to be here.
Host: Let's start with a strange word. What's nomophobia?
Doctor: It's short for no mobile phone phobia. I'm sure many listeners are familiar with this feeling. It's the fear of being without your phone.
Host: Is it a big problem in the United States?
Doctor: Well, about nine in ten American adults have a smartphone, so a lot of people can feel it. And in my office I'm seeing an increase in the number of patients who are worried about it.
Host: How do I know if I'm nomophobic?
Doctor: Ask yourself some questions. Do you feel nervous when your battery is low? Do you check your phone every few minutes? Do you take it into the bathroom? People with this problem hate any separation from their phone. They're afraid of losing contact with the world.
Host: OK, I think we have a caller. Hi Lucy, you're on Chicago Talks!
Lucy: Hi! Thanks for taking my call. So... I take my phone everywhere. Into the shower, into class, to bed. Last week I lost it on the bus, and I felt terrible for two hours. Is that normal?
Doctor: Thanks for calling. It's very common, but it isn't healthy. Why do you think you need it all the time?
Lucy: I'm a student, and I work at a coffee shop on weekends. I'm always in contact with my friends, my boss and my family. I'm afraid of missing something important.
Doctor: That's one of the main reasons for this problem. We call it FOMO, the fear of missing out. But here's the good news. There's a simple solution to it. Make some rules. For example, no phone at dinner and no phone in the bedroom.
Lucy: No phone in the bedroom? But it's my alarm clock!
Doctor: Buy an old alarm clock. They're cheap!
Lucy: Ha! OK, I'm tired of feeling this way, so I'll try it. Thank you!
Host: Good luck! So Doctor, why are you so interested in this topic?
Doctor: Because sometimes it's dangerous. Many people read messages while they're driving. In twenty twenty-three, distracted driving killed three thousand two hundred and seventy-five people in the United States. We're all responsible for how we use our phones.
Host: That's a serious number. Thank you for coming. And listeners, put your phone away... after the show!
